paragraphs.heading: The Atlantic's deepest place
paragraphs.text: The Puerto Rico Trench runs parallel to and north of Puerto Rico, on the boundary between the North Atlantic Ocean and the Caribbean Sea. It holds the deepest points in the Atlantic. It is 810 km long, with a maximum recorded depth of between 8,376 and 8,740 m. The deepest spot is usually called the Milwaukee Deep, while Brownson Deep names the seabed around it, though lately both names have been used for the point itself. In 2018 the ship DSSV Pressure Drop located that point with multibeam sonar, and Victor Vescovo then piloted the crewed submersible Limiting Factor down to it and confirmed its depth.

paragraphs.heading: Plates sliding past
paragraphs.text: Two plates meet at the trench and mostly slide past one another along a transform boundary. Only a little subduction, one plate sinking under another, happens there. The Caribbean plate moves east relative to the North American plate, and at the trench the North American plate is pushed down at a slant beneath the Caribbean plate. Farther southeast, the South American plate goes down more directly along the Lesser Antilles subduction zone, which explains the active volcanoes in the southeastern Caribbean. NASA reports that a very dense mass beneath the trench bends gravity enough to make the ocean surface dip somewhat. It also makes navigation instruments less accurate.

paragraphs.heading: Quiet volcanoes, real danger
paragraphs.text: Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, Hispaniola, Cuba and Jamaica began as part of a volcanic arc but have no active volcanoes today. Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands have had none for about 30 million years. The islands still face earthquakes and tsunamis. The trench has produced earthquakes above magnitude 8.0 and is thought able to do so again. Its subduction zone has not ruptured in more than 200 years, which worries geophysicists who think it may be due for a major event.

paragraphs.heading: Past shocks
paragraphs.text: On 11 October 1918 a major earthquake hit western Puerto Rico and caused a tsunami; it came from an old strike-slip fault near the Mona Passage. Studies conclude that a quake along the trench's fault zone could also set off a significant tsunami. Tremors in and around the island are frequent. In January 2014 a magnitude 6.4 earthquake north of Puerto Rico came from oblique-thrust faulting, where the North American plate moves about 20 mm a year relative to the Caribbean plate.

paragraphs.heading: Getting ready
paragraphs.text: Many people on the islands near the trench have not known about these risks. Since 1988 the Puerto Rican Seismic Society has used local media to warn of a future quake that could be catastrophic. After the 2004 tsunami, which affected more than 40 countries around the Indian Ocean, many more people fear such an event in the Caribbean, and local governments have begun emergency planning. For Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, the United States government is expanding its seismic studies and developing tsunami warning systems.

paragraphs.heading: Life on the trench floor
paragraphs.text: The French bathyscaphe Archimède first reached the floor in 1964, and a robotic vehicle followed in 2012. Its video was dominated by swarms of amphipods living on the bottom. Some, caught in bait bags, turned out to be Scopelocheirus schellenbergi, a species otherwise found only in ultradeep Pacific trenches. The video also showed a sea cucumber 10 to 20 cm long, tentatively placed in the genus Peniagone, and a 3 cm isopod later identified as Bathyopsurus nybelini.
